passage:
Friday: At Varun's farewell from the office, Jyoti threw her arms round him without thinking. He went rigid and stepped back, smiling awkwardly. Jyoti felt her face burn.
Saturday: She messaged him. 'Sorry about yesterday. I should have asked.' He replied, 'Thanks for saying that. In my family we don't really hug. And after some things growing up, I'm careful about it. Nothing to do with you.'
The following Friday: They met for coffee before he left the city. When they said goodbye, Jyoti asked, 'Hug, handshake or wave?' Varun grinned. 'Handshake, with feeling.' They shook hands warmly, and he said, 'That meant a lot, you asking.'

qa.q: What did Jyoti do at Varun's farewell?
qa.a: She threw her arms round him without thinking.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when Varun stepped back?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, with her face burning.

qa.q: What did Jyoti change the following Friday, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She asked 'Hug, handshake or wave?', which let Varun choose and made the goodbye feel warm and safe.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt when Jyoti asked first?
qa.a: He felt respected and touched, saying it meant a lot.

grounding: Shows a caring person learning to ask before hugging, accepting a no without offence and finding another warm way to say goodbye.

passage: Ayesha, beti, you're sulking because your new friend won't hug you back? Let your Devika Khala tell you something. When I was your age, I had a friend at work called Farzana. Whenever I hugged her, she went stiff as a board. I was hurt. I thought she didn't like me. For months I kept hugging her, thinking she'd warm up. Then one day she told me, very quietly, that in her home touching was rare, and that some old things made hugs frightening for her. I felt terrible. I had never asked. After that I always asked, 'Hug or no?' Mostly she said no. So instead I brought her cutting chai every morning and saved her a seat. She came to my wedding and cried. We're still friends, forty years later.

qa.q: What did Devika bring Farzana every morning?
qa.a: Cutting chai.

qa.q: How did young Devika feel when Farzana stiffened at hugs?
qa.a: She felt hurt and thought Farzana did not like her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Devika's story?
qa.a: Farzana explaining why hugs were hard, after which Devika always asked first and showed warmth in other ways.

qa.q: How might Farzana have felt when Devika kept hugging her?
qa.a: Farzana probably felt uncomfortable and even frightened, but unsure how to say so.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a person learning to ask before hugging, accepting a no, and finding other ways to show warmth shaped by a friend's history.

passage: The big wheel at the Pushkar fair creaked and glittered. Gautam, five, held his father's hand tightly. 'Papa, my tummy's funny. Like something's flapping inside.' Kamal crouched. 'Flapping? That sounds like butterflies. Lots of people get butterflies in their tummy when they're nervous or excited.' Gautam thought. 'Both?' 'Maybe both.' Kamal put Gautam's hand on his chest. 'Is your heart going fast too?' Gautam nodded. 'That's your body telling you, this is a big thing.' Gautam looked up at the wheel. 'Can we go on the small swings first?' 'Good idea.' On the swings, Gautam laughed, and said, 'The butterflies are flying away.'

qa.q: What did Gautam say was flapping inside?
qa.a: Something in his tummy.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he looked at the big wheel?
qa.a: He felt nervous and excited, with butterflies in his tummy and a fast heart.

qa.q: What did Kamal do to help Gautam understand his body?
qa.a: He named the flapping feeling as butterflies and linked it to feeling nervous or excited.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt when Gautam chose the small swings?
qa.a: He was probably pleased that Gautam listened to his body and chose a smaller step.

grounding: Shows a young child linking a fluttery tummy and fast heart to nervousness and excitement, with a parent naming these body signals.

passage: After a long afternoon in a Madrid park, Mateo, five, sat on the pavement and refused to walk. 'My legs are broken!' Rania knelt beside him. 'Are they broken, or are they heavy?' Mateo thought. 'Heavy. Like sandbags.' 'Heavy legs usually mean our body is tired. Is your face feeling hot too?' He touched his cheeks. 'Yes.' 'Hot face and heavy legs. Your body is saying: rest and a drink, please.' He gulped from the water bottle and leaned against her on the bench. Soon he said, 'My legs are a bit less sandbag now,' and walked home holding her hand.

qa.q: What did Mateo say his legs felt like?
qa.a: Heavy, like sandbags.

qa.q: What was Mateo feeling when he refused to walk?
qa.a: He was tired and cross, feeling his legs were broken.

qa.q: How did Rania help Mateo understand what his body was saying?
qa.a: She named heavy legs and a hot face as signs of tiredness and needing rest and a drink.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt when Mateo sat down on the pavement?
qa.a: She may have felt a little impatient, but chose to kneel and help him understand.

grounding: Shows a young child learning to link heavy legs and a hot face to tiredness, with a parent naming these body signals.

passage: In the kindergarten art corner, Siddharth, five, knocked over the paint pot. Blue paint splashed across Riya's picture. Everyone looked. Siddharth's face went bright red, and he hid under the table. Zeenat Teacher crouched down beside him. 'Siddharth, is your face feeling hot?' A tiny nod. 'Sometimes when we feel embarrassed, our face gets hot and we want to hide. That's your body telling you.' He peeked out. 'Embarrassed?' 'That's the word. It's okay. We can fix the picture together.' Siddharth crawled out slowly. He helped Riya turn the blue splash into a sky. His face cooled down, and he even smiled.

qa.q: What did Siddharth knock over?
qa.a: The paint pot.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he hid under the table?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, with a hot, red face and a wish to hide.

qa.q: What did Zeenat Teacher do that helped Siddharth understand?
qa.a: She named his hot face as a sign of feeling embarrassed and offered to fix the picture together.

qa.q: How might Riya have felt when the paint splashed on her picture?
qa.a: Riya was probably upset at first, then pleased when they turned it into a sky.

grounding: Shows a young child linking a hot face to embarrassment, with a teacher naming the body signal so he understands what is happening inside.

passage: When I was ten, I spent a whole Sunday building a castle from blocks at my aunt Seema's flat. I didn't stop for lunch. I didn't drink water. I didn't go to the toilet, even though I sort of needed to. Around five, the tower fell over, and I completely fell apart. I screamed, kicked the blocks, and then realised I desperately needed the toilet and ran. I'm Gargi, and I remember Seema Maasi afterwards, handing me a sandwich. 'Your body was shouting at you all afternoon,' she said. 'You just didn't hear it.' She set a little timer on her phone. 'Every hour, when it rings, you ask: am I hungry, thirsty, do I need the loo?' I thought it was silly. But I used it the next Sunday, and I didn't fall apart.

qa.q: What did Gargi build at Seema Maasi's flat?
qa.a: A castle from blocks.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when the tower fell?
qa.a: Gargi felt furious and overwhelmed, falling apart after hours of ignoring hunger and needing the toilet.

qa.q: What did Seema Maasi teach Gargi to do?
qa.a: To check every hour when a timer rang: am I hungry, thirsty, do I need the loo?

qa.q: How might Seema Maasi have felt watching the meltdown?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and concerned, then understood Gargi had ignored every body signal all afternoon.

grounding: Shows a child absorbed in play ignoring hunger, thirst and a full bladder until everything falls apart, and a regular body check building awareness.

passage:
Art club note, Wednesday
Tanuja, eight, loves painting and gets completely absorbed. Twice this month she has suddenly burst into tears near the end of the session, and both times she urgently needed the toilet and had to run. Today she also said her head hurt, and admitted she hadn't eaten her snack. I think she simply doesn't notice her body's signals while she's focused. So at the halfway mark, I now ring a little bell and the whole group does a 'body check': toilet, water, snack if needed. Tanuja giggled about it, but she went to the toilet and ate her fruit, and she finished her painting calmly. I'll keep the bell going.
Jomon, art club leader

qa.q: What does Jomon ring at the halfway mark?
qa.a: A little bell.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling when she burst into tears near the end?
qa.a: She was upset and uncomfortable, suddenly overwhelmed by needing the toilet and being hungry.

qa.q: What change did Jomon make, and why does it help?
qa.a: A halfway 'body check' bell for the whole group, which gives Tanuja a regular pause to notice her needs.

qa.q: How might the other children feel about the body check?
qa.a: They probably find it a bit funny but useful, and Tanuja does not feel singled out.

grounding: Shows a child absorbed in an activity missing hunger and toilet signals until she falls apart, and a regular body check building awareness.

passage:
Saturday
Played cricket with Divyansh from nine till four. Best day ever until about three, when I suddenly felt awful. My head was pounding, my mouth was dry, and I got so angry when I got out that I threw the bat and shouted at Divyansh. He just said, 'Did you even eat?' I hadn't. Not lunch, not water, nothing. I'd been too busy playing to notice. When I got home, Mummy gave me water and food, and I felt normal again in half an hour. Then I felt bad about shouting.
Tomorrow's plan: after every innings, quick body check. Hungry? Thirsty? Toilet? Divyansh says he'll remind me. Also I'll say sorry.
Nilesh

qa.q: How long did Nilesh play cricket?
qa.a: From nine till four.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel around three o'clock?
qa.a: Nilesh felt awful, with a pounding head and dry mouth, and angry enough to throw the bat.

qa.q: What is Nilesh's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: A quick body check after every innings for hunger, thirst and the toilet, with Divyansh reminding, and saying sorry.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt when Nilesh shouted?
qa.a: Divyansh was probably surprised and a bit hurt, but guessed Nilesh was hungry.

grounding: Shows a child absorbed in play missing hunger and thirst until everything falls apart, and planning quick body checks to build awareness.
